messages.subject: shrinkage in Lavaan
parts:
Hello, 

I'm trying to better understand the role of the general statistical concept "shrinkage" in SEM. From what I've been able to understand, what are typically called shrinkage estimators in multilevel modeling are most commonly marginal maximum likelihood (MML) or empirical Bayes estimators. I've seen that Lavaan recent introduced an MML estimator for SEM. However, the Mplus creators have stated that the maximum likelihood robust (MLR) estimator is equal to Bock's MML (http://www.statmodel.com/discussion/messages/9/10401.html?1427253381). If Lavaan already has an MLR estimator that is equivalent to MML (per Mplus), can your provide some more information on the difference between MML and MLR? I'm sure this is a straightforward topic but I seem to get always get lost in the terminology. 

Thanks!
Garett

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: shrinkage in Lavaan
parts:
A late reply:

MLR is Mplus speak for 'robust' ML. This means that the estimation is
vanilla ML, but the inference (standard error, goodness of fit) is robust.

So, when we only talk about estimation, MLR is just plain ML.

MML is also ML, but refers to a specific approach that is used in the
context of categorical data. In this setting, can either 'integrate out'
the latent response (y*) variables (this is estimator = FML, but totally
useless), or we can integrate out the latent variables; the latter is
(in the IRT literature) usually called 'marginal ML'

Mplus calls this 'ML(R)', but lavaan does not.

In lavaan, MML can only be used in the categorical setting (with latent
variables), while ML(R) can only be used in the continuous setting.

Yves.
